W7214897514.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have substantially advanced natural language generation (NLG), but high-quality content creation remains constrained by hallucination, limited controllability, retrieval noise, domain shift, and computational cost. This study proposes Retrieval-Augmented and Preference-Aligned Generation (RAP-Gen), a unified framework that integrates retrieval-augmented generation, factual preference alignment, in-context learning, and denoising pre-training. The framework combines a dense semantic retriever with an encoder–decoder generator, introduces pairwise factual-preference supervision for controllable generation, aligns retrieval and generation distributions, and uses structured text corruption to improve robustness to incomplete or noisy inputs. Experiments are reported on summarization, long-form creative writing, and knowledge-intensive question answering using CNN/DailyMail, WritingPrompts, Natural Questions, and general language-modeling data. The reported results show that RAP-Gen improves ROUGE, BERTScore, perplexity, FactScore, and human-rated factuality relative to the baselines listed in the manuscript. Ablation results indicate that removing retrieval, preference alignment, or denoising degrades performance, supporting the complementary roles of external knowledge, preference signals, and robust pre-training. Additional analyses examine the number of retrieved documents, attention over retrieved evidence, robustness under input perturbation, model scaling, and in-context learning. Because the supplied material does not include raw predictions, code, repeated-run variance, annotator agreement statistics, or complete benchmark configurations, the numerical results are interpreted as reported experimental outcomes rather than independently reproducible evidence. The study contributes an integrated design for knowledge-grounded, preference-aware content generation and identifies evaluation and reproducibility requirements for future work.

W7215051446.abstract: We present the results of \textbf{MADGRAV}, a deep-learning-based search for high-mass compact binary coalescences, applied to the data collected by the LIGO interferometers during the third observing run and during the first and second part of the fourth observing run. The \textbf{MADGRAV} pipeline consists of a series of sequential convolutional neural networks that perform anomaly detection, glitch classification, coherence testing, and signal ranking. Data from the Hanford and Livingston LIGO detectors are studied (both individually and in coherence) by way of 1 second Q-transform windows. Of the candidates that survive every stage of the pipeline, 48 reach the significance threshold, and we report 47 gravitational wave detections characterised by a false alarm rate below $1\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ with a probability of astrophysical origin $p_{\rm astro}>0.9$. Of the 47 detections, 44 are shared with the minimally modelled coherent WaveBurst search. The observed total source-frame masses, extracted from official gravitational wave transient catalogues, are in the $14-236 M_{\odot}$ range with a median of $69 M_{\odot}$, and a median SNR of 16. We note that the recovered fraction of confident detections rises with mass: for LIGO detectors network SNR $>10$ the pipeline recovers $8.1\%$ of confident catalog events below $30 M_{\odot}$, $39.8\%$ between $30$ and $100 M_{\odot}$, and $53.3\%$ above $100 M_{\odot}$, corresponding to $33.3\%$, $45.5\%$ and $53.3\%$ of the events detected by coherent WaveBurst in the same bins. These results suggest that anomaly detection pipelines can serve as an independent detection channel complementary to matched filtering in the high-mass high-SNR regime.

W7215083141.abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) remains a significantly challenging task for low-resource, morphologically rich languages such as Tamil due to the scarcity of annotated dataset and linguistic complexities. While large transformer-based models have advanced multilingual NLP capabilities, they often fall short when applied directly to such languages. This paper proposes a hybrid architecture that combines the deep contextual embeddings from a pre-trained XLM-ROBERTa model with a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) decoder to enhance sequence-level dependency modeling for Tamil NER. We train and evaluate the model on the publicly available Naamapadam dataset. The proposed approach achieves a token-level F1-score of 78.8%, demonstrating a significant improvement of over 5.4% compared to the established IndicNER benchmark and other baseline models. Qualitative analysis further confirms the model’s robustness in handling ambiguous entities and complex sentence structures, validating the effectiveness of combining multilingual transformers with lightweight sequential decoders for low-resource languages.

W7215094343.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly combined with knowledge graphs (KGs) to ground reasoning in structured evidence. However, most LLM-based KGQA methods rely on traversing existing graph edges and become unreliable when reasoning paths are broken by missing facts. Alternatives that ask LLMs to generate missing knowledge risk introducing hallucinated evidence. We introduce XoG (eXplore-over-Graph), a framework for multi-hop question answering over incomplete KGs that recovers missing reasoning paths from learned graph structure rather than LLM parametric knowledge. XoG combines type-level entity-relation statistics to identify candidate relations with KG embeddings to retrieve plausible missing entities, using the LLM as a semantic selector and reasoner. These mechanisms are integrated into an iterative planning-exploration-reasoning process. Experiments on WebQSP, CWQ, and the Wikidata-based BRINK benchmark show that XoG remains competitive on complete KGs and consistently outperforms comparable methods without task-specific KGQA training under KG incompleteness. These gains persist across multiple LLM backbones, indicating that stronger LLMs alone do not resolve missing graph evidence. XoG also reduces LLM token consumption by up to 33% compared with a closely related planning-based approach.

W7215568581.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence has introduced new possibilities for building intelligent support systems, particularly inhealthcare environments where continuous guidance is essential. This study presents a multi-agent AI frameworkdesigned to assist patients during the post-discharge phase. The proposed system combines Retrieval-AugmentedGeneration with an agent-based architecture to deliver context-aware and reliable responses.The framework consists of two specialized agents: a Receptionist Agent that manages communication and user-specificdata, and a Clinical AI Agent responsible for domain-level reasoning. By grounding responses in verified medicalinformation and discharge records, the system reduces the likelihood of incorrect outputs and improves trust. Theresults suggest that an agent-oriented approach enhances system flexibility, scalability, and safety in healthcareapplications..

W7215946550.abstract: Contextual security defenses prevent AI agents from taking rogue actions by synthesizing a task-specific policy and enforcing it on the agent's tool calls. In multi-step tasks, however, which actions are valid often depends on what the agent has already done and learned. We present Sapien, a policy engine for enforcing stateful contextual policies. A Sapien policy specifies permitted tool-call sequences using a regular expression extended with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks. We show that Sapien stays within a few percent of an unconstrained agent's utility. Even if the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies rule out 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon (twice as many as tool allowlists on long-horizon tasks).

W7216417419.abstract: Controlling database systems using traditional interfaces requires a strong understanding of Structured Query Language (SQL) and the database administration tools employed. This study introduces a new AI-based system that automates create, read, update, and delete database actions through natural language processing, supporting multiple natural languages and diverse user vocabularies. The fundamental architectural innovation of this research consists of developing a bridge between Google's Gemini Large Language Model and the Google Agent Development Kit, referred to as the Gemini-Agent Development Kit Bridge. While the Agent Development Kit is built on a set of structured commands and handles all database query execution, Google's Gemini serves as a smart communication layer between the user and the Agent Development Kit. Thus, the main responsibility of Gemini is the translation from the entire range of natural language used by the user into a structured command recognizable by the Agent Development Kit, regardless of its vocabulary, informality, or language. In the same way, the output of the Agent Development Kit is transformed into human-readable output by Gemini. The proposed solution was designed as a Flask-based e-commerce management system and evaluated using 325 manually authored test cases covering five operational classes. On average, 93.8% accuracy was achieved for the translation of commands, with an accuracy of 96.0% for order deletion and 87.5% for complex multi-step operations. The response time varied between 1.2 seconds for simple commands and 3.5 seconds for complex operations. This finding has substantial implications, as it suggests that Gemini's broad natural-language capabilities can be employed to expand access to structured backend systems without altering the execution layer.

W7217487099.abstract: A Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) is a type of health information technology that helps doctors and nurses make clinical decisions. Health information technology (HIT), especially clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) that work with electronic health records (EHRs), can help people make more consistent judgments based on evidence. There have been many published examples of CDSS success stories in the last ten years or more. CDSS has evolved as an essential component in contemporary healthcare, thereby altering the method in which medical professionals make decisions, with the goals of enhancing clinical decision-making, improving patient outcomes, and optimizing healthcare delivery. CDSSs can help in diagnosis, treatment, patient management, and prevention, which can lead to better patient outcomes, fewer medical errors, and better quality. Clinicians generally use modern CDSS solutions at the point of care, where the system gives them data-driven insights and suggestions that help them improve their skills. Priorities include investing in strong IT infrastructure, extensive training programs, and public awareness campaigns, as well as making CDSSs work better with EHR platforms. India can use CDSSs to improve patient care and outcomes if government agencies, healthcare institutions, and technology suppliers work together to remove these impediments. Overall, CDSS is a big step forward for smart healthcare systems. It makes clinical workflow more efficient and helps patients get better results. Finally, it is evaluated with two datasets from the UCI repository, and its performance is high in deep learning when compared with the other techniques in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity.

W7219696267.abstract: Cancer remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide despite substantial advances in molecular diagnostics, targeted therapeutics, immunotherapy, and precision medicine. The extraordinary biological complexity of malignant diseases, together with rapidly expanding volumes of clinical, radiological, pathological, genomic, and molecular data, has created increasing demand for intelligent computational systems capable of supporting individualized clinical decision-making. Recent developments in agentic artificial intelligence (AI) have introduced a new generation of autonomous clinical systems that extend beyond conventional predictive models by continuously perceiving, reasoning, planning, acting, and learning from dynamic healthcare environments. Unlike traditional AI systems that perform isolated prediction tasks, agentic AI integrates multimodal biomedical information, electronic health records, medical imaging, genomic sequencing, digital pathology, laboratory biomarkers, wearable technologies, and clinical guidelines to autonomously coordinate diagnostic reasoning, therapeutic planning, longitudinal monitoring, and adaptive decision support under physician supervision. Advances in large language models, foundation models, multimodal learning, graph neural networks, reinforcement learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and autonomous AI agents have accelerated the development of intelligent oncology ecosystems capable of supporting cancer diagnosis, molecular characterization, treatment optimization, immunotherapy prediction, adaptive radiation therapy, clinical trial matching, survivorship management, and precision therapeutics. Despite these advances, important challenges remain regarding explainability, algorithmic reliability, interoperability, ethical governance, cybersecurity, regulatory approval, accountability, and safe clinical implementation. This review provides a comprehensive overview of agentic artificial intelligence in precision oncology, highlighting computational foundations, current clinical applications, emerging innovations, and future perspectives for autonomous clinical decision systems across the cancer care continuum.[1]

W7220141406.abstract: One of the key non-classical resources involved in the promise of quantum computing is quantum entanglement. It allows for correlations between qubits that are not possible by independent local states, thus it can be used for computational speed-up, quantum simulation, quantum error correction, quantum machine learning, and secure quantum communication. This paper explores the role of entanglement in quantum computing, and looks at its applications with a secondary-data based research design. This study will evaluate the progress of entanglement from a fundamental physical phenomenon to an engineering resource for processors, algorithms, and fault-tolerant architectures from peer-reviewed literature, institutional reports and public research data from 2018 to 2025. The paper is divided into five subheadings in the introduction, four subheadings in the literature review, a research methodology, and a results section with five secondary-data tables, and a conclusion. The findings reveal a significant acceleration in noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices between 2018 and 2025, along with efforts to prove quantum computational advantage, grow of variational algorithms and increased advancement toward logical qubits and quantum error correction. The evidence also shows that there are important limitations for practical quantum benefit, including decoherence, errors in quantum gates, difficulties loading data, benchmarking arguments, and the high cost of overhead error correction in fault-tolerant quantum computing. The authors conclude that entanglement is not just a theoretical property of quantum physics, but the resource that is needed to link hardware and software with applications. In the future, fidelity of entangling gates, scalable qubit connectivity, error-mitigated algorithms, and fault-tolerant logical qubit designs will all be important.

W7220188527.abstract: The exponential growth of scholarly output and the advent of generative artificial intelligence have intensified demands for scalable, accurate verification of academic content, encompassing plagiarism detection, citation accuracy, factual consistency, and identification of AI-generated text. This review examines automated verification systems powered by domain-specific large language models (LLMs), framing them as intelligent engineering systems (IES) that enhance research integrity within academic publishing ecosystems. Grounded in systems engineering, cyber-physical systems (CPS) theory, and information theory, these frameworks leverage fine-tuned scientific language models, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and cross-modal analysis of text, figures, and citation networks. The analysis delineates four AI-driven transformation pathways: from generic, standardized screening tools to personalized, discipline-specific verification; from reactive post-submission detection to proactive risk forecasting during manuscript development; from labor-intensive manual curation to autonomous intelligent pipelines; and from isolated software modules to integrated cyber-physical ecosystems linking authors, editors, reviewers, and institutional repositories. Concrete examples include domain-specific LLMs such as SciBERT and BioBERT augmented with RAG for citation context verification, and graph-based models for detecting anomalous citation patterns. While these systems markedly improve throughput and consistency, they introduce risks of hallucination, training-data bias, and adversarial manipulation. Future trajectories emphasize knowledge-grounded architectures, multi-agent verification ensembles, and digital-twin representations of the scholarly communication process. The work supplies a rigorous foundation for developing trustworthy, domain-aware verification technologies aligned with broader IES principles.

W7220275258.abstract: The increasing environmental impact of fossil fuel consumption has accelerated interest in sustainable energy carriers, with green hydrogen emerging as a key option for decarbonization. This review critically evaluates the current status of green hydrogen production technologies, including alkaline water electrolysis (AEL), proton exchange membrane electrolysis (PEMEL), anion exchange membrane electrolysis (AEMEL), and solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOECs). Reported system efficiencies range from approximately 60–70% for conventional alkaline systems to over 80% for advanced SOEC technologies under optimized conditions. Recent advances in electrocatalysts, membrane materials, and renewable energy integration have improved system performance; however, challenges related to capital cost, durability, scalability, hydrogen storage, and transportation remain significant barriers to large-scale deployment. The review further highlights emerging research directions, including hybrid electrolysis systems, artificial intelligence-assisted optimization, and advanced catalyst development. Overall, green hydrogen demonstrates strong potential to support deep decarbonization and long-term energy storage, although continued technological innovation and cost reduction are required for widespread commercialization

W7220693119.abstract: Language models exhibit strong reasoning capabilities, yet adapting them to structured domains remains challenging and can yield inconsistent outcomes. We identify representation compatibility, the extent to which a model effectively processes a representation for a structured task, as a key factor in adaptation. We study this in chess, which provides a controlled testbed with precise semantics, computable optimal actions, and multiple state representations, including a symbolic encoding (FEN) and a spatial format (ASCII). We find that models often process semantically equivalent inputs substantially differently, affecting both learning and generalization. Building on this observation, we propose representation-aligned auxiliary supervision, which uses environment-derived tasks expressed in compatible representations to improve adaptation to structured domains. Across models and representations, auxiliary supervision consistently improves optimal-move prediction relative to target-only training under identical target data. Tasks that expose environment dynamics provide larger and most consistent gains than surface-level or static supervision, while remaining competitive with substantially increasing the amount of target-task data. Moreover, ASCII-trained models transfer more effectively to FEN than FEN-trained models do to ASCII, even surpassing the FEN target-only baseline on FEN evaluation. The gains also extend beyond optimal-move prediction to open-ended, factually grounded commentary generation. Overall, our results show that auxiliary supervision in model-compatible representations can enable effective adaptation in structured domains.

W7220704589.abstract: Generative large language models (LLMs) inherit undesirable behaviors from pre-training, including demographic bias and toxic generation, that often emerge only after deployment and affect a small subset of inputs. A repair should eliminate the identified defect, preserve the model's overall functionality and, ideally, provide correctness guarantees. Existing approaches address this only partially: gradient-based fine-tuning lacks per-instance guarantees and becomes unstable with few defect samples; model editing assumes explicit knowledge replacement rather than behavioral correction; and constraint-based repair is largely restricted to discriminative models with unique target outputs. We present FORGE, a framework for targeted behavioral repair of generative language models that separates defect localization, weight editing, and behavioral verification into independent stages. Its core is a repair abstraction that converts localized defective generation into explicit optimization objectives, enabling verification-oriented repair techniques to operate on autoregressive generation. FORGE is editing-mechanism agnostic: we instantiate it with (1) a constraint-based quadratic optimization method that provides per-sample repair certificates and (2) a null-space projection editor that minimizes interference with the original model distribution, both under the same localization and verification protocol. On five open-source LLMs, FORGE consistently achieves larger reductions in bias and toxicity than gradient-based fine-tuning with minor perplexity degradation. The two backends exhibit complementary performance across architectures, which a lightweight causal probe traces to where toxicity-related signals concentrate. FORGE also remains effective with only a handful of defective examples, where conventional fine-tuning often oscillates or fails to converge.

W7220721796.abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, the emergence of various Large Language Models (LLMs) has created a rich model ecosystem. However, this also brings a key challenge: how to select the optimal model for a specific user query. LLM routing addresses this need by dynamically assigning queries to the most suitable expert in the pool of candidate models. However, existing routing frameworks often simplify this process to a standard classification task; thus, a critical vulnerability is exposed when multiple candidate models correctly answer the same query. We formalize this capability overlap as routing noise, which misleads the router with arbitrarily correct candidate models, ultimately leading to routing collapse (a severe decline in generalization ability on unseen tasks). To address this problem, we propose a novel Cluster-Aware Soft-Labeling Routing (CASLR) framework. CASLR shifts the evaluation paradigm from the success of a single query to macro-domain consensus by replacing traditional one-hot vectors with a masked softmax mechanism. Specifically, for experts who answer incorrectly, we penalize their target probability to zero; for the remaining candidates, we directly compute continuous fine-grained soft labels based on their global clustering utility scores. We then use these refined soft labels to supervise a lightweight router. Specifically, the framework not only demonstrates superior accuracy on multiple benchmarks, but also outperforms Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct by 7.80% in overall average performance. Furthermore, the extremely low routing inference latency of only 1.13s further confirms that CASLR can achieve efficient system scheduling with almost zero additional overhead, while ensuring high response quality.

W7221020680.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) hold the promise of order-agnostic, parallel text generation. Recently, continuous diffusion and flow matching models have seen substantial gains, driven by carefully crafted token representations and diffusion/flow spaces. In this work, we introduce Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (H-CDLMs), a simple framework that further improves continuous DLMs with minimal compute and parameter overhead. Drawing on the discrete DLM and continuous image diffusion literature on joint diffusion, we diffuse multiple modalities in parallel. These modalities represent tokens at different semantic granularities: in our instantiation, the tokens themselves and coarser clusters obtained by clustering pretrained token embeddings. We propose a general setup that allows per-modality samplers and schedules to enhance the interplay between modalities. Applied to CoBit, this yields H-CoBit, which delivers large empirical gains across benchmarks. At dataset entropy, H-CoBit improves MAUVE and reaches a generative perplexity (GenPPL) of 49.4 on LM1B and 50.4 on OWT, improving on the baseline by 24.2 and 20.7 points and surpassing even discrete DLMs of comparable size. On GSM8K, it reaches 27.4% accuracy, outperforming prior continuous diffusion and flow-based models. We further apply H-CDLM to the flow matching model FLM, obtaining consistent gains with H-FLM and demonstrating that the framework generalizes across continuous generative paradigms. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/matol-16/HCDLM.git .

W7221045580.abstract: Three-dimensional organoid systems have transcended their role as exploratory research tools to emerge as transformative platforms for mechanistic pharmacology, biomarker discovery, and precision therapeutics. These self-organized multicellular structures, derived from patient-derived stem cells or engineered pluripotent stem cells, recapitulate organ-level complexity including metabolic competency, barrier function, and disease-specific phenotypes. This review examines the convergence of organoid technology with artificial intelligence, high-throughput phenotypic screening, and multi-organ microphysiological systems—collectively enabling systems-level pharmacological modeling previously impossible in traditional experimental contexts. We discuss novel applications in acquired drug resistance, patient stratification, biomarker-driven therapeutic selection, and mechanism-of-action studies. Critically, we analyze the emerging paradigm of “organoid-based personalized medicine circuits” integrating patient genetics, organoid-derived phenotypes, and computational modeling to predict therapeutic responsiveness. Current regulatory frameworks, standardization efforts, and pathways toward clinical integration are examined, positioning organoid pharmacology as a defining methodology for next-generation drug development.

W7221100712.abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) workflows remain strongly dependent on expert decisions in geometry preparation, meshing, model and solver configuration, convergence assessment, post-processing, and design iteration. This review examines agentic artificial intelligence (AI) for CFD automation and engineering design, with emphasis on reinforcement learning (RL) agents and large language model (LLM) agents. RL agents provide rapid, task-specific, and physics-aware execution within predefined observation and action spaces, whereas LLM agents offer flexible goal interpretation, knowledge access, planning, and tool orchestration. To organize these potentially complementary capabilities, a unified taxonomy is introduced based on decision paradigm, CFD role, and degree of autonomy, while multi-agent organization is treated as a separate architectural property. The reviewed evidence indicates that neither RL nor LLM agents alone are sufficient for trustworthy autonomous CFD. A hierarchical autonomous-CFD-engineer architecture is therefore proposed, combining an LLM orchestrator, domain-specialized agents, conventional CFD tools, independent numerical and physical verification, shared provenance, and human governance. Extending this architecture toward hypothesis formulation, numerical-experiment design, and model discovery suggests a pathway to an AI CFD scientist; however, current systems support bounded automation and supervised scientific collaboration rather than independent scientific judgment.

W7221118669.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) impacts the brain in multiple ways and has varied clinical features and progression. Sex differences exist in the epidemiology and fundamental biology of AD. Machine learning (ML) tools can integrate and analyze multiple biomarkers, improving AD diagnosis and prognosis. However, machine learning tools underuse and under-explore predictive modeling of sex differences. This translational narrative review synthesises the existing literature on studies that explore sex differences in Machine Learning models that utilise data collection techniques that incorporate biomarkers from Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans, Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF), serum assays, genetic variants, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and Electroencephalography (EEG). We emphasize the role of sex in biomarker manifestations which include but are not limited to: the dissimilarity of amyloid and tau in PET imaging, the effects of sex in structural and functional brain alterations in MRI, sex-specific alterations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) composition (e.g., Aβ42 concentration, total tau, and phospho-tau) and the alterations in peripheral and systemic inflammatory and metabolic blood markers, the modulation of genetic risk particularly in relation to APOE and some of the single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and the variability in sex differences in EEG network disruption and/or modularity. When sex is incorporated as a biological variable or when sex-stratified models are created, new ML methods, such as deep learning, ensemble techniques, and multimodal fusion frameworks, demonstrate promising diagnostic and prognostic capabilities. Many studies, however, remain constrained by modest datasets, a lack of external validation, and limited interpretability, thereby limiting clinical applicability. This review highlights the importance of sex-aware modeling techniques to advance precision medicine in AD. We offer several methodological suggestions, including analysing disaggregated sex data, aligning data across multiple approaches, using explainable AI, and including longitudinal data. Filling these gaps may help develop ML tools that offer accurate, fair, and clinically useful early detection and prognosis of AD across a wide range of populations.

W7221156795.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most challenging malignancies due to profound biological heterogeneity, complex stromal organization, and limited responsiveness to current immunotherapies. Recent advances in single-cell sequencing, spatial omics, digital pathology, and multimodal profiling have revealed that PDAC immune states are shaped not only by cellular composition but also by spatial organization, treatment context, and patient-specific evolutionary trajectories. However, the increasing complexity and fragmentation of biomedical evidence create substantial challenges for conventional artificial intelligence (AI) approaches that are typically optimized for predefined analytical tasks. Autonomous AI research agents represent an emerging paradigm that extends beyond predictive modeling by integrating scientific reasoning, retrieval of heterogeneous biomedical knowledge, computational tool orchestration, workflow adaptation, and evidence traceability. In this Review, we examine how agentic AI systems may contribute to PDAC immunology research, from characterization of immune ecosystems and spatial cellular interactions to biomarker discovery, neoantigen prioritization, and experimental protocol design. We distinguish AI agents from conventional task-specific models and discuss essential capabilities required for reliable biomedical research, including planning, tool use, verification, memory, provenance tracking, and human oversight. Despite promising technical demonstrations in biomedical domains, direct evidence supporting fully autonomous AI-driven discovery and validation in PDAC remains limited. Therefore, we propose a disease-oriented evaluation framework emphasizing benchmark task design, appropriate human and computational comparators, reproducibility assessment, and experimental validation. Future PDAC-specific AI research agents should prioritize evidence-aware reasoning, multimodal integration, calibrated uncertainty, and transparent computational-experimental workflows. Such systems may ultimately accelerate mechanistic discovery and precision immunology, while maintaining rigorous standards for biological validity, reproducibility, and responsible scientific practice.

W7221587549.abstract: Autoregressive large language models (LLMs) are bottlenecked by sequential decoding, where each new token typically requires executing all transformer layers. Existing dynamic-depth and layer-skipping methods reduce this cost, but often rely on auxiliary routing mechanisms or incur accuracy degradation when bypassed layers are left uncompensated. We present LoRA-Drop, a post-hoc adaptable inference framework that accelerates decoding by applying atemporal compute scheduleto a fixed subset of intermediate layers: on most decoding steps, selected layers reuse the previous-token hidden state and apply a low-rank LoRA correction, while periodicrefreshsteps execute the full model to prevent drift. LoRA-Drop requires no routing network, is compatible with standard KV caching, and can reduce KV-cache footprint by skipping KV updates in droppable layers during LoRA steps and refreshing periodically. Across LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B, LoRA-Drop achieves up to 2.6× faster decoding and 45–55% KV-cache reduction while staying within 0.5 percentage points (pp) of baseline accuracy. Evaluations on reasoning (GSM8K, MATH, BBH), code generation (HumanEval, MBPP), and longcontext/multilingual benchmarks (LongBench, XNLI, XCOPA) identify a consistentsafe zoneof scheduling configurations that preserves quality while delivering substantial efficiency gains, providing a simple path toward adaptive-capacity inference in LLMs. Codes are available athttps://github.com/hosseinbv/LoRADrop.git.

W7221718400.abstract: Abstract A persistent gap separates academic research priorities from the operational challenges faced by manufacturing firms. Established identification methods, among them Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) workshops, Lean audits and consultant engagements, are episodic, bounded by participant expertise and organised along departmental lines, which makes cross-departmental issues hard to surface. Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) have meanwhile shown collaborative problem-solving ability in software engineering and, more recently, in shopfloor scheduling and supply chain coordination. This article is a Perspective. It develops a framework and a research agenda; implementation and empirical evaluation fall outside its scope and are set out as its first research priorities. Three contributions are offered. The first is a synthesis of literature from industrial problem identification, LLM-based autonomous agents and manufacturing AI, which positions the proposal against existing industrial LLM agent work. The second is a framework in which six domain-specialised agents (production, quality, maintenance, supply chain, safety, energy) would collaborate through a five-phase protocol: worker-driven discovery, cross-departmental analysis, candidate-relationship detection, consensus-based financial assessment and debate-driven prioritisation. The prioritisation procedure is fully specified, including the normalisation of financial estimates, a measure of estimate dispersion, the derivation of criteria weights, a non-compensatory gate for safety-critical items and a mandatory human verification step. The third is a worked calculation on a hypothetical steel manufacturing vignette, included so that the procedure can be reproduced and scrutinised rather than as evidence of effectiveness. A preliminary qualitative readiness assessment and a three-horizon agenda of fourteen research questions complete the paper. The benefits identified are presented as hypotheses for that agenda to test rather than as demonstrated outcomes.

W7221832364.abstract: Experiments with remote decision-making agents depend on more than the policy: the world may change during inference, the simulator determines which actions are available, and births and immigration alter who can act. We present Jevolution, an instrumented spatial predator-prey framework that makes these dependencies explicit. Its reference implementation separates the evolving world, asynchronous request scheduling, controller adapters, and experiment records. The model combines local observations, energy and resource constraints, predefined signals, and inherited scalar traits. We describe these mechanisms using the ODD protocol and distinguish implemented controls from research questions requiring additional interventions. Free synthetic fixtures exercise scheduling, signaling, and inheritance against the pinned implementation; they validate specified software behavior rather than model intelligence or ecological realism. A completed communication case study illustrates the end-to-end workflow using Jev to control both species. Across 6 complete habitat-seed pairs, the mean signals-on minus signals-off difference in normalized rabbit abundance was -0.0095 (nominal 95% pair-bootstrap interval [-0.0772, 0.0602]). This small study does not resolve the direction of the signal-system effect. The contribution is an inspectable experimental system and its evidence boundaries, not a new policy-learning algorithm or a demonstration of emergent language, adaptive selection, or biological predictive validity.

W7222554667.abstract: Repeated Bertrand competition is a stringent benchmark for algorithmic pricing: in homogeneous-goods markets, standard learning procedures typically select the stage-game Nash outcome with prices near marginal cost. We show that LLM pricing agents can escape this benchmark, depending on deployment decisions. LLMs outperform standard online learners through faster adaptation, but this advantage largely disappears against full-information learners. An extracted surrogate algorithm illustrates how LLMs in specific deployments profit from regularly undercutting slower learners. Agents that post one price every period from raw market histories that include rival prices can sustain supracompetitive regimes in self-play. Agents that periodically emit probability distributions from summarized histories of their own profits instead move toward the competitive region in self-play. Markets mixing these interfaces can generate dynamic regimes in which LLMs establish a high-price anchor and regularly undercut it to capture demand. These regimes can keep both competitors' prices above marginal cost. Deployment choices shape these outcomes, shifting the focus from stationary equilibria to dynamic pricing regimes.

W7222628263.abstract: Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) embeds large language models (LLMs) in action loops in which they plan, retrieve evidence, invoke tools, maintain memory, coordinate with other agents, and change external state. Reviews of this field have proliferated, yet they remain fragmented: architecture surveys catalogue components, evaluation surveys catalogue benchmarks, and safety surveys catalogue risks, while deployed agents couple all three. Scholars have yet to sufficiently examine how capability, evaluation, and governance interact within the lifecycle of a single agentic system. We address this gap through a critical review that codes 19 reviews and surveys published in Artificial Intelligence Review between 2024 and 2026 and situates them within foundational primary studies and cross-venue surveys. We argue that agency is a configurable property of a socio-technical control loop, not an attribute of a model. From the corpus, we develop the Agentic Intelligence Lifecycle (AIL), a six-layer framework spanning foundation, cognition, grounding, orchestration, evaluation, and governance. Our central finding is that every mechanism that expands capability also incurs an assurance debt : a gap between the risks the mechanism introduces and the controls that keep those risks observable and bounded. We theorize this relationship in five propositions, propose a five-question assurance model that shifts evaluation from outputs to trajectories and deployment conditions, and derive a ten-point research agenda for agentic systems that are observable, attributable, interruptible, and governable.

W7222870850.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into educational, professional, and technological environments, creating opportunities for innovation while raising concerns regarding transparency, accountability, ethical responsibility, privacy, and governance. Despite the growing use of AI-powered technologies among university students, limited research has examined how engineering students perceive corporate governance practices associated with these technologies. This study explored the perceptions of undergraduate engineering students regarding corporate governance in AI-powered technologies. A descriptive quantitative research design employing a cross-sectional survey approach was utilized. Data were collected from ninety-two (92) undergraduate engineering students at Cebu Institute of Technology–University (CIT-University) using a structured questionnaire. Frequency counts, percentages, weighted means, and ranking procedures were used to analyze the data. The findings revealed that respondents demonstrated positive awareness of corporate governance principles in AI systems, particularly regarding ethical responsibility, accountability, transparency, and data governance. The respondents also expressed a generally favorable level of trust in organizations utilizing AI-powered technologies, although concerns regarding privacy protection, data security, and responsible AI implementation remained evident. Among the governance dimensions examined, accountability received the highest rating, followed by ethical governance and transparency. Furthermore, the results showed that engineering students generally practiced responsible AI use, particularly in avoiding technologies that violate ethical and privacy standards. Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude, were identified as the most commonly used AI-powered technologies among the respondents. The study concludes that engineering students recognize the importance of responsible AI governance and view accountability, ethical responsibility, and transparency as essential components of trustworthy AI systems. These findings may contribute to the development of governance policies, educational initiatives, and responsible AI practices within academic and technological environments.

W7222947711.abstract: Code review generation can reduce developer effort by producing concise, reviewer-style feedback for a given code snippet or code change. However, generation-only models often produce generic or off-point reviews, while retrieval-only methods struggle to adapt well to new contexts. In this paper, we view retrieval augmentation for code review as retrieval-augmented in-context learning: retrieved historical reviews are placed in the input context as examples that guide the model’s output. Based on this view, we propose RARe (Retrieval-Augmented code Reviewer), a framework that retrieves relevant historical reviews from a corpus and conditions a large language model on the retrieved in-context examples. Experiments on two public benchmarks show that RARe outperforms strong baselines and reaches BLEU-4 scores of 12.32 and 12.96. A key finding is that more retrieval can hurt: using only the top-1 retrieved example works best, while adding more retrieved items can degrade performance due to redundancy and conflicting cues under limited context budgets. Human evaluation and interpretability analysis further support that retrieval-augmented generation reduces generic outputs and improves review focus.

W7223045463.abstract: External skills provide language-model agents with reusable procedural knowledge, yet how models use such knowledge after it is supplied remains poorly understood. We identify Procedural Exposure Bias (PEB), the tendency of language models to increasingly favor an action as its associated procedural pattern is repeatedly exposed in a skill, even when the interaction state and action relevance remain unchanged. We find that PEB strongly depends on how procedural knowledge is represented: presenting the same content visually substantially attenuates exposure-induced shifts in action preference relative to textual presentation. Further analysis shows that this attenuation primarily arises from visual encoding rather than structured layout. Although repeated procedural signals remain recoverable from Visual representations, they exert a weaker influence on downstream action prediction, distinguishing signal accessibility from its use as action evidence. This effect also extends to executable action selection, where increasing exposure more strongly favors the corresponding action under Text than Visual. Layer-wise analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence becomes more pronounced toward the model output, with stronger evidence under Text, while activation interventions reveal architecture-specific roles of internal components in transmitting or counteracting the preference shift. Complete-agent evaluations across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop further show that Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all four evaluated models. These findings establish skill representation as an important factor governing how procedural knowledge is translated into agent decisions. All code is available at https://github.com/NEUIR/Vis-Skill.

W7223063000.abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

W7223175164.abstract: The Large Language Model (LLM) is a sophisticated artificial intelligence system designed to think and react in ways very close to how humans do in their minds. Its primary focus is on understanding users' intentions, breaking complex questions into simpler parts, and delivering accurate and insightful responses in a concise format. To improve its performance over time, it uses reasoning, memory, and learning skills. The Mental LLM is designed to deliver quick, accurate, and secure results across a range of fields, including data analysis, customer service, education, and health care support. It improves communication and problem-solving skills by mimicking human-like cognitive processes, including logical decision-making, memory, and step-by-step thinking. The increasing reliance on AI systems for routine tasks requires not only accurate but also "contextual" responses closer to human reasoning. To improve human-AI interaction, this project proposes a Mental Reasoning-Driven Large Language Model (LLM) that integrates cognitive reasoning into conventional language models. The system can interpret users' intentions, understand context, and deliver accurate responses through a combination of symbolic reasoning, neural networks, and knowledge integration. Applications in the fields of education, healthcare, customer support, and decision-making can benefit from the model's capability to adapt to user interactions, maintain multi-turn dialogues, and provide personalised interactions. This method bridges conventional AI responses with human-like comprehension. Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed the dynamics of human-AI interactions. The practicality of LLMs in real-world scenarios is limited by their inability to perform deep reasoning and learning. To create a model that mimics human thought processes, a Mental Reasoning-Driven Large Language Model is proposed.

W7223176843.abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) is routinely reported following colorectal cancer resection, although the implications of a positive finding are not uniform and depend on tumor site, stage, treatment setting, and accompanying risk features.We conducted a focused narrative review of records in PubMed/MEDLINE covering the period from January 1, 1975 through June 30, 2026, together with backward and forward citation tracking.The review centered on three issues: (1) Whether PNI provides prognostic information beyond TNM stage and established clinicopathological variables; (2) Whether PNI identifies differential benefit from adjuvant therapy; and (3) Whether preoperative imaging, radiomics, artificial intelligence, or biomarker-based methods have reached a level of validation sufficient to inform research-oriented or guidelineconcordant multidisciplinary consideration.Overall, the literature most consistently identifies PNI as an unfavorable postoperative prognostic factor, particularly in stage II-III colorectal cancer.Its additional prognostic value, however, appears to vary once lymphovascular invasion, tumor budding, nodal involvement, molecular characteristics, and treatment response are considered.In stage II colon cancer, PNI may lend additional weight to an individualized discussion of adjuvant chemotherapy, but observational evidence has not shown a reproducible treatmentby-PNI interaction.Persistent PNI in rectal cancer, particularly after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, is likewise associated with poorer outcomes and should be interpreted in conjunction with ypTNM stage and the degree of treatment response.Classification systems based on invasion depth or spatial distribution are biologically reasonable, but their definitions remain inconsistent across studies.Preoperative computerized tomography-based and magnetic resonance imagingbased predictive models have shown moderate to high discriminatory performance in several reports; nevertheless, their retrospective nature, variable reference standards, and limited prospective validation currently restrict their use to researchoriented risk assessment rather than model-directed management.Circulating and tissue-based biomarkers remain similarly investigational.From a clinical 4 / 61 perspective, PNI should therefore be reported consistently and incorporated as a weighted component of multidisciplinary risk assessment rather than used in isolation as a justification for treatment intensification.

W7223358348.abstract: This paper explores the emerging phase of enterprise transformation driven by the transition from traditional AI automation tools to autonomous and semi-autonomous agentic AI systems. While generative AI and large language models (LLMs) have enhanced productivity in cognitive tasks and isolated workflows, systemic enterprise transformation remains uneven. To address this challenge, we propose a three-dimensional conceptual framework linking: (1) technical agent capabilities (reasoning, planning, and cross-system orchestration); (2) organizational readiness (data infrastructure maturity, process modularity, and human-AI collaboration); and (3) governance mechanisms (autonomy regulation, accountability, and risk containment). Furthermore, we discuss the coordination challenges of multi-agent ecosystems, cybersecurity, and ethics, including accountability diffusion and algorithmic drift. By conceptualizing AI agents as socio-technical actors, this study frames intelligent transformation as an organizational design challenge for achieving sustained competitive advantage.

W7223660915.abstract: The growing complexity of modern energy systems, driven by renewable energy integration, distributed energy resources, electric vehicles (EV), and intelligent infrastructures, has increased the need for autonomous and adaptive energy solutions. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled the emergence of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI), which combines reasoning, planning, tool utilisation, and autonomous decision-making through intelligent agents. Despite increasing interest in this paradigm, its application in intelligent energy systems remains fragmented and lacks a comprehensive review. This study presents an early-stage review of the emerging literature on Agentic AI for intelligent energy systems. Bibliometric analysis was conducted to examine publication trends, keyword frequency, term co-occurrence patterns, geographical distribution, and collaboration networks. A qualitative content analysis was subsequently performed to evaluate application domains, methodologies, strengths, limitations, and key findings. The results show that Building Energy and Demand-Side Management is the dominant application area, followed by Power Systems and Smart Grids, Energy Markets and Trading, Electric Mobility and Charging Systems, Renewable Energy Systems, and Energy AI Platforms and Operations. Multi-agent architecture and LLM-based reasoning emerged as the most widely adopted approaches, often integrated with digital twins, reinforcement learning (RL), knowledge graphs (KGs), and optimisation frameworks. While Agentic AI demonstrates significant potential for intelligent energy systems, challenges related to scalability, interoperability, trustworthiness, and real-world deployment remain. The study concludes by identifying key research gaps and proposing future directions for the development of trustworthy and autonomous energy systems.

W7223666679.abstract: The advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing both in terms of understanding and generating language across various applications. But applying them to other specific areas like healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, legal systems, engineering and scientific research often results in limited contextual understanding of the domain, ambiguous terms, and inconsistent knowledge. This paper presents the idea of Domain-Specific Knowledge Acquisition and Representation based on a Contextual Language Modeling (CLM) framework which aims to improve the contextual reasoning by using adaptive domain-aware language modeling. The proposed framework combines the various components of domain-specific corpus construction, semantic contextual embedding, transformer-based contextual encoding, dynamic knowledge augmentation and retrieval-enhanced generation to generate accurate and contextually relevant responses. The hybrid attention mechanism, along with contrastive representation learning, allows the model to handle complex semantic relationships, while minimizing the hallucination and knowledge consistency issues. Moreover, it introduces an adaptive prompt optimization strategy and an iterative domain adaptation module to enable it to seamlessly learn new knowledge and avoid retraining the entire model. Experimental testing is carried out on several benchmark datasets in the fields of healthcare, cybersecurity, finance, and scientific literature. Proposed approach is compared with the state-of-the-art transformer-based language models on the basis of the following evaluation metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, BLEU, ROUGE-L, BERTScore, Hallucination Rate, Context Consistency Score and Inference Latency. The results show that the proposed model provides a better contextual understanding, domain knowledge representation, response reliability, and less computational overhead than the other models. The proposed contextual language modeling framework is effective and scalable for intelligent knowledge systems, which are domainspecific, and can be extended to future AI driven Decision Support, Knowledge Management and Enterprise Information retrieval systems.

W7223672557.abstract: Maintenance reports are a rich source of information for reliability engineering and asset management.They typically contain unstructured text and categorical information, which can be used to estimate quantities of interest for maintenance decisions, such as Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) of system components.However, the extraction of knowledge from these reports is challenged by linguistic variability, technical jargon and frequent human errors committed when filling the categorical fields.To address these issues, the present work proposes a novel, two-step method based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically identify the units, subunits and components involved in maintenance interventions.First, an LLMbased model ( ) identifies possible quality issues in the unstructured text, flagging reports that suffer from brevity, lack of context, excessive use of technical terms, internal incoherence and inconsistencies with the categorical fields.Then, based on an equipment taxonomy, a second LLM-based model ( ) systematically identifies the units, subunits and components involved in the maintenance interventions from reports of low quality.The overall method is validated considering a real-world case study of maintenance reports from a mining haul truck fleet.The obtained results demonstrate that: i) successfully identifies quality issues in a significant fraction (36%) of the reports; ii) effectively corrects erroneous categorical assignments of the units, subunits and components involved in the maintenance intervention in low quality reports.

W7223852971.abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous AI agents has brought about significant progress in the field of intelligent systems that can reason, plan, and use tools. Yet, current agentic frameworks are mostly autonomous task pipelines that are poorly coordinated, have poor memory and have suboptimal execution strategies. In this paper, the authors present an Agentic AI Operating System (AAIOS), which is an operating-system inspired orchestration to support autonomy of multi-agent workflows. The design includes a dynamic agent scheduling component, persistent memory management, inter-agent communication, and task monitoring, all encapsulated as a unified design to coordinate specialized agents capable of complex tasks. The architecture of AAIOS is modular; it includes a Planner Agent, execution agents specific to the different tasks, a two-level memory subsystem, and a dependency-aware scheduling layer. The system uses FastAPI, LangGraph for scalable, autonomous execution, Redis for communication, and vector memory storage. Experimental results in three different task domains show that the proposed multi-agent architecture provides a Task Completion Rate of 91.4% against the single-agent baseline of 74.2% and a Memory Utilization Efficiency of 0.67 and a close linear scaling with throughput of 8 concurrent task streams.

W7223993082.abstract: High-fidelity digital twins in continuous biomanufacturing are often bottlenecked by incomplete kinetic models, while standard data-driven algorithms (e.g., SINDy, PINNs) lack interpretability or impose rigid physical assumptions. This paper introduces a hybrid closed-loop architecture for autonomous kinetic state-space discovery driven by a Large Language Model (LLM) agent. The framework employs a sequential "isolation-peeling" methodology across orthogonal operational regimes. This algorithmic peeling mathematically decouples entangled multiplicative (inhibitory) and additive (catalytic) biological rate law. Grounded in a Two-Level Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) library, the framework utilizes Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) and logarithmic decomposition to decouple complex cell growth kinetics into orthogonal multiplicative (inhibitory) and additive (regulatory) residual channels. When statistical degeneracy occurs an Active Design of Experiments (DoE) controller dynamically triggers targeted perturbations to decorrelate competing model hypotheses. Evaluated on a continuous stirred-tank reactor exhibiting unmodeled Haldane inhibition, Luong product toxicity, and secondary metabolite autocatalysis, the framework autonomously expanded the state space and recovered ground-truth parameters with under 6% error without a priori kinetic knowledge.

W7224735380.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly acting through Web interfaces and external tools. They produce trajectories. Those trajectories may pass through several intermediaries. They can store, modify, or dispute those trajectories. In Web-based agent deployments, trajectories may pass through APIs, marketplaces, and tool servers. As such, a copied or disputed log may not by itself reveal which agent owner produced it. Behavioral watermarking can embed ownership evidence in agent action choices. However, existing methods mainly address detection, removal, rewriting, or imitation. They do not directly test whether repeated observation of watermarked trajectories enables cross-session forgery by exploiting learned action preferences. We formulate this learned-forgery threat and propose AgentAnchor, a session-keyed behavioral watermark for owner attribution from trajectory logs. We derive each step key from a secret key, a fresh public session identifier, and semantic states of recent observations, while a guarded digest of the action-policy state diversifies linear coding rows. It embeds parity evidence through a KL-bounded exponential tilt, and a trusted verifier checks a disputed log without rerunning the agent, using wrong-key calibration and abstention.

W7224757071.abstract: With the increase in diabetic population, there is a pressing need for doctors to address this issue. Autonomously managing complex healthcare tasks, reducing human error and enhancing efficiency is the striking characteristic of Agentic AI. It is imperative to provide a personalized treatment plan in medical management of diabetes or in prevention of prediabetic individuals from being diabetic whichever the case may be. The delivery of personalized treatment plan in diabetes care is a highly anticipated benefit of integrating Artificial Intelligence with Clinical Decision Support System. This research aims to explore the design, validation, and deployment of Agentic AI systems capable of transitioning from advisory roles to autonomous clinical actions. This proposed work includes Agentic Artificially Intelligent Agents which are trained using Federated Learning. Optical Character Module that accepts glucose reading from medical reports (OCR module) has been proposed. Depending on the glucose reading from reports, the agents predict whether the person has diabetes. A Multi Agent team collaboratively works in diabetes prediction and detection. Furthermore, a Small Language Model suggests personalised dietary recommendations. In this paper, we present a proactive based Agentic AI framework for diabetes prediction that collaboratively unifies structured knowledge with predictive model and autonomous decision support. The implementation of Agentic AI framework as proposed in this paper has been deposited in the following GitHub repository. https://github.com/aaeshasultana-ops/AI-Ninjas#ai-ninjas

W7224814602.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.

W7224916342.abstract: The rapid digital transformation of financial and public welfare systems has created a growing demand for intelligent and autonomous pension management platforms capable of handling large-scale operations efficiently and securely. The traditional pension service systems are generally plagued with slow processing, manual verification dependence, security concerns, poor scalability, and the inability to make real-time decisions. In order to overcome these drawbacks, the paper presents an autonomous pension service operations environment based on multi-agent artificial intelligence architecture, providing distributed intelligent agents for beneficiary verification, pension calculation, detecting fraud, coordination of the service workflow, data analytics, compliance monitoring, and customer interaction. The proposed framework provides support for multiple AI agents interacting with one another, which enhances the effectiveness of workflows, decreases the latency of operations, and decreases the amount of human involvement in the process. To provide superior fraud prediction, operational optimization, and intelligent pension processing, machine learning-based analytical models are embedded. Moreover, cloud-based infrastructure and secure communication systems make it possible for scalability, transparency, and system reliability. Based on the experimental results, it can be concluded that the proposed framework can accurately classify the data with an accuracy of nearly 95.83%, which is greater than the traditional pension management approach and can effectively improve flow coordination, fraud prevention ability, service reliability, and resource utilization. The findings show that the proposed system is able to offer an efficient, secure, and scalable backbone for future AI-enabled autonomous pension service ecosystems.

W7225015259.abstract: Artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and business analytics are increasingly converging to support automated financial decision making, yet integrated frameworks combining business intelligence with taxation remain limited. This study develops an autonomous cloud-based decision-support framework integrating agentic AI, business analytics, Income Tax intelligence, and GST intelligence. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data processing, business analytics, banking analysis, tax screening, GST rule evaluation, anomaly detection, orchestration, and decision support. Empirical evaluation used integrated commercial and banking records to assess sales, profitability, payment behavior, cash flow, and transaction-risk indicators. Results showed total sales of ₹437,771, recorded profit of ₹36,963, bank credits of ₹420,570.51, and bank debits of ₹422,089.90. UPI represented 45.07% of integrated records, while anomaly screening identified 152 high-value sales observations and 135 high-value banking transactions. Income Tax and GST outputs were generated as rule-based intelligence indicators rather than statutory assessments because direct return variables were unavailable. The proposed architecture demonstrates the feasibility of combining autonomous agents, cloud-enabled analytics, financial monitoring, and tax-oriented screening while retaining explainability, auditability, and human oversight for consequential decisions. The framework provides a scalable foundation for future enterprise deployment, real-time integration, and compliance-oriented financial intelligence applications.

W7225049967.abstract: Wearable medical devices integrated with artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming chronic disease management by enabling real-time health monitoring. Despite advances, gaps remain in predictive analytics and seamless integration into clinical workflows. This review addresses these challenges by evaluating AI-driven wearables for early intervention in conditions like diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and respiratory disorders. Methods include a systematic analysis of current devices, focusing on biosensor technology, machine learning algorithms, and agent-based orchestration for data processing and regulatory compliance. Key findings reveal that AI wearables, such as continuous glucose monitors, reduce hospital readmissions by 30% and improve patient adherence by 25% in recent studies. Edge computing and cloud-based systems enhance real-time decision-making, while agent-based frameworks ensure data security under HIPAA and GDPR. However, issues like algorithmic bias and limited clinical validation hinder widespread adoption. The review proposes a scalable integration model for wearables within digital health ecosystems, emphasizing interoperability and cost reduction. These advancements could save healthcare systems $200 billion annually by 2030 while empowering clinicians with actionable insights. This work highlights AI wearables as a cornerstone of precision medicine, driving proactive care and improved outcomes for chronic disease patients.

W7225063742.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an increasing global healthcare challenge that reduces the effectiveness of antibiotics and complicates the treatment of infectious diseases. Conventional microbiological diagnosis and antimicrobial susceptibility testing remain essential for identifying bacterial pathogens and selecting appropriate treatments; however, delays in obtaining results may contribute to inappropriate antimicrobial use. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, genomic analysis, and advanced diagnostic technologies offer promising approaches to improving pathogen identification, resistance prediction, antimicrobial discovery, and clinical decision-making. This narrative review discusses the potential integration of AI with rapid diagnostic platforms, whole-genome sequencing, antimicrobial stewardship, and bacteriophage therapy. AI-based models can assist in analysing complex microbiological data, identifying resistance-associated patterns, and prioritising potential antimicrobial candidates. In parallel, bacteriophages offer a complementary therapeutic approach against selected bacterial infections, including infections caused by multidrug-resistant organisms. Nevertheless, limitations involving data quality, model generalisability, clinical validation, cost, regulatory oversight, and healthcare infrastructure remain significant barriers. The integration of AI with established microbiological methods could support faster and more informed treatment decisions when appropriately validated. This review highlights the need for interdisciplinary collaboration among microbiologists, clinicians, data scientists, and public health professionals to translate emerging technologies into accessible and clinically reliable AMR management strategies.

W7225084075.abstract: Agentic AI systems can pursue objectives over multiple steps, determine intermediate actions, use tools, adapt to changing circumstances and act with reduced human intervention. This publication examines what these capabilities could mean for international peace and security. It distinguishes agency from autonomy and assesses how agentic capabilities are emerging across cybersecurity, military command and control, and autonomous physical systems. The evidence remains uneven: the clearest current examples are found in cyber and other digital environments, while military applications in command and control and physical systems remain more experimental. The publication also examines risks including misalignment, error propagation, constraint circumvention, loss of human control and interactions between agents operated by different actors. For international peace and security, these developments could compress decision time and reduce opportunities for human clarification and de-escalation, particularly as agents operated by different actors increasingly interact. This is especially important where existing crisis-management arrangements rely on human signalling, interpretation and restraint. Rather than assuming that agentic AI requires an entirely new governance regime, the publication argues for stress-testing existing legal and policy frameworks, strengthening practical controls and assurance, and beginning international dialogue on agent-to-agent interactions before such practices become widespread.

W7225091749.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence, a.k.a. agentic AI, is an emerging area that has gained popularity for its ability to plan, reason, and act independently. Agentic AI is an orchestration system that supervises and coordinates multiple models and agents to handle broader and more complex goals. It is built on existing agent technologies, but the implementation is different and more powerful than earlier agent systems that commonly use rules, rationalities and policies to reason in limited environments. Current agentic AI systems can dynamically plan in open real-world systems and reason using multiple agents, such as rule-based systems, reinforcement learning agents, and large language model agents. However, agentic AI systems may not fully capture users’ intentions. To improve decision quality, this paper investigates the role of the human in current agentic AI systems to determine how the user as a decision maker interacts with the system. We present an empirical study of the human user and compare the design of these systems with actual practice. We find that although leading agentic AI systems have hybrid decision-making processes with a ‘human-in-the-loop’ (HIL) where autonomous workflows pause at critical decision points to request human validation, guidance, or approval before proceeding, users often bypass their control points and allow the system to run asynchronously (referred to as YOLO or ‘you only live once’). We extend the research to develop a typology of HIL (Human-In-the-Loop), HOL (human-on-the-loop), and HOOL (human-out-of-the-loop) in collaboration with a senior engineer developing agentic AI systems and applications in a leading Fortune 500 technology company, together with a decision support expert, to present an empirical representation of the current state of human-agentic AI systems. The paper also sheds light on issues with agentic AI, such as user misdirection and suggests research opportunities.

W7225146488.abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.
